scenes.visual: Title card: How Life Remade the Planet.

scenes.tts: For most of its history, life on Earth was microbial. Rocks 3.48 billion years old in Western Australia hold what researchers read as traces of microbes in hot springs. Then life remade the planet. Oxygen began to build up in the air by about 2.4 billion years ago. Many-celled algae appear just over a billion years ago, animals by about 558 million, and plants on land by about 470 million. And five times, mass extinctions swept away most species.
scenes.visual: A single timeline runs left to right. Mounds labelled Dresser appear at 3.48 billion years; the sky above the line turns from orange to blue at the oxygen marker; a red alga, a Dickinsonia outline and a small land plant drop onto the line at their dates; five red notches cut the right-hand end.

scenes.tts: The Great Oxidation Event was the first big buildup of oxygen in the air. It was not the start of oxygen-making photosynthesis. With oxygen, aerobic metabolism spread. An ozone layer would have shielded life near the surface from ultraviolet light. And living things had to cope with oxygen's harm.
scenes.visual: Oxygen dots accumulate in the sky above a shallow sea; a thin ozone band forms and deflects violet rays; cells below light up with an aerobic label, and a few show a red warning glow.

scenes.tts: A mass extinction is the loss of more than three quarters of species in a geologically short time. At the end of the Cretaceous, 66 million years ago, the evidence converged. Iridium, rare in Earth's crust but common in many meteorites, is enriched at the boundary at widely separated sites. A buried crater, Chicxulub, lies in Mexico. Dating puts impact and extinction within 32,000 years. The impact triggered the extinction.
scenes.visual: Three rock columns on a world map each light a gold iridium band at the same level; a crater outline appears under the Yucatan; two dated layers join with a gold bracket labelled synchrony.

scenes.tts: The end of the Permian, about 252 million years ago, was the largest loss in the marine record, about 81 percent of marine species by one estimate. At Meishan in China, dated ash beds show the dying there took about 60 thousand years, with wide uncertainty. That is a clock for one place. Any proposed cause has to fit it.
scenes.visual: A grid of marine species icons greys out to about four in five; then a single rock column labelled Meishan with ash bands and a short bracket marking the extinction interval.

scenes.tts: Extinctions also open space. Placental mammals diversified mainly after the end-Cretaceous extinction. That timing fits release from competitors, but does not prove it. A flask can test the logic. Rainey and Travisano grew one genotype of the bacterium Pseudomonas in still broth. New heritable types filled different zones. In shaken broth, they did not. These were new types, not new species.
scenes.visual: Mammal branches fan out just after a red extinction line; then two flasks side by side: the still one layered, with a gold mat on top and different cell shapes at depth; the shaken one uniform with only smooth cells.

scenes.tts: How do we know when? Zircon in volcanic ash is a mineral clock: uranium decays to lead at a steady rate. Ash beds above and below a fossil bracket its age. But the oldest fossil is only a floor. Life existed by 3.48 billion years ago; it may be older.
scenes.visual: A zircon crystal with orange uranium dots turning green; a rock column with ash above and below a fossil bed and a yellow bracket; the Dresser marker returns with a red dashed zone opening to the older side.

scenes.tts: So the history of life is transitions that remade the planet, extinctions that cleared it, and radiations that filled it again, each dated by rocks, with fossil dates telling you only when, at the latest.
scenes.visual: The full timeline from s01 returns with three chips: transitions, extinctions, radiations; ends on the take-home line.
